questions.stem: Which result confirms ammonia?

options.text: Damp red litmus paper turns blue
options.explanation: That is the official ammonia test result.

options.text: Damp blue litmus paper bleaches white
options.explanation: That is the chlorine test, not the ammonia test.

options.text: Limewater turns cloudy
options.explanation: Cloudy limewater identifies carbon dioxide.

options.text: A glowing splint relights
options.explanation: A relighting splint identifies oxygen.

questions.stem: Why must the litmus paper avoid touching the tube sides when testing gas from ammonium ions and sodium hydroxide?

options.text: The paper must stay dry to work
options.explanation: Litmus paper needs to be damp for the gas to dissolve into it.

options.text: Traces of sodium hydroxide on the glass would also turn the paper blue
options.explanation: The alkali solution itself would give a blue result, so contact would fake a positive.

options.text: The glass would cut the paper
options.explanation: The concern is chemical, not mechanical.

options.text: Sodium hydroxide would bleach the paper white
options.explanation: Bleaching is chlorine's behaviour; sodium hydroxide turns litmus blue.

questions.stem: What two changes does chlorine make to damp blue litmus paper?

options.text: Bleaches it white with no colour change first
options.explanation: The red stage is part of the mark; skipping it loses the sequence.

options.text: Turns it green, then blue
options.explanation: Neither colour belongs to the chlorine test.

options.text: Turns it red, then bleaches it white
options.explanation: Red first as acids form, then white as the bleach takes hold.

options.text: Turns it blue, then bleaches it red
options.explanation: The paper already starts blue, and the sequence is reversed nonsense.

questions.stem: Why does the litmus turn red before bleaching?

options.text: The chlorine itself is an alkali
options.explanation: An alkali would turn red litmus blue, which is ammonia's behaviour.

options.text: The paper dries out during the test
options.explanation: Drying is not the mechanism; reaction with water is.

options.text: Ammonia is also present
options.explanation: No second gas is needed to explain the red stage.

options.text: Acids form when chlorine reacts with the water on the paper
options.explanation: The damp paper supplies water, and the acids made turn blue litmus red before bleaching follows.

questions.stem: A gas smells like swimming pools. Can it be identified as chlorine on that evidence?

options.text: No, a smell is a property, not an acceptable identification test
options.explanation: Characteristics such as smell describe a gas but cannot certify it.

options.text: Yes, smell is definitive for chlorine
options.explanation: Smell alone never identifies a gas in exam answers.

options.text: Yes, if the smell is strong
options.explanation: Strength of smell changes nothing about identification standards.

options.text: No, because chlorine is odourless
options.explanation: Chlorine does have a sharp choking smell; the rejection is for the wrong reason.
options.misconception: wrong fact attached to right conclusion

questions.stem: State the colour change seen when damp red litmus paper is held in ammonia gas.
questions.modelAnswer: The damp red litmus paper turns blue.

questions.stem: State the two-stage observation produced by chlorine on damp blue litmus paper, in order.
questions.modelAnswer: Chlorine turns the damp blue litmus paper red first and then bleaches it white.

questions.stem: Explain why the litmus paper must not touch the glass sides during the ammonium-ion test.
questions.modelAnswer: Sodium hydroxide traces clinging to the glass would also turn red litmus blue, giving a false positive; only the gas above the solution should be sampled.

questions.stem: Gas X turns damp red litmus paper blue; gas Y turns damp blue litmus paper red and then white. Identify both gases.
questions.modelAnswer: Gas X is ammonia and gas Y is chlorine.

questions.stem: What is limewater?

options.text: Copper(II) sulfate solution
options.explanation: That is the water-test reagent, unrelated to limewater.

options.text: Calcium hydroxide solution
options.explanation: Limewater is the common name for dissolved calcium hydroxide.

options.text: Sodium hydroxide solution
options.explanation: Sodium hydroxide is an alkali reagent but not limewater.

options.text: Calcium carbonate suspension
options.explanation: Calcium carbonate is the white solid made during the test, not the starting liquid.

questions.stem: What positive result does carbon dioxide give with limewater?

options.text: The limewater turns blue
options.explanation: Blue belongs to litmus and copper compounds, not to limewater.

options.text: The limewater fizzes
options.explanation: The gas is being bubbled in already; the observation is the cloudiness.

options.text: The limewater turns cloudy white
options.explanation: Insoluble calcium carbonate forming in the liquid makes it cloudy.

options.text: The limewater turns clear again
options.explanation: The starting liquid is already clear; the change is towards cloudiness.

questions.stem: A student says a burning splint went out, so the gas is carbon dioxide. Why is this wrong?

options.text: Splints never go out in any gas
options.explanation: Splints do go out in unreactive gases; that is exactly the problem.

options.text: Only hydrogen extinguishes splints
options.explanation: Hydrogen is the gas that pops, not the one that merely goes out.

options.text: Carbon dioxide relights splints
options.explanation: Relighting belongs to oxygen; carbon dioxide extinguishes.

options.text: Other gases such as nitrogen also extinguish a splint
options.explanation: Extinguishing a flame is shared behaviour, so it cannot name the gas.

questions.stem: Why is limewater described as the definitive carbon dioxide test while the splint test is not?

options.text: Only carbon dioxide turns limewater cloudy, while several gases extinguish flames
options.explanation: Specificity is what makes a test an identification test.

options.text: Limewater reacts with every gas
options.explanation: Limewater is selective; reacting with everything would make it useless.

options.text: The splint test works only in daylight
options.explanation: No daylight condition exists for splint tests.

options.text: Cloudiness is easier to see than flame
options.explanation: Convenience is not what makes a test definitive; exclusivity is.

questions.stem: Gas X bubbles through limewater, which stays clear. What follows?

options.text: The limewater must have been pure water
options.explanation: Blaming the reagent is not justified when the method was followed.

options.text: X is not carbon dioxide
options.explanation: A clear result rules out carbon dioxide, though it names nothing instead.

options.text: X is definitely nitrogen
options.explanation: A negative carbon dioxide test does not confirm any other specific gas.

options.text: X is definitely hydrogen
options.explanation: Hydrogen has its own splint test; nothing here proves it.

questions.stem: State the chemical identity of limewater.
questions.modelAnswer: Limewater is calcium hydroxide dissolved in water, so it is a calcium hydroxide solution.

questions.stem: Describe the appearance change that counts as a positive limewater result.
questions.modelAnswer: Bubbling the gas through limewater turns the limewater cloudy white.

questions.stem: Explain why an extinguished splint is not accepted as a test for carbon dioxide.
questions.modelAnswer: Other gases such as nitrogen also extinguish a burning splint, so a flame going out is a shared property and identifies none of them specifically.

questions.stem: Two unknown gases are bubbled through separate limewater samples; one sample turns cloudy and the other stays clear. State what each result shows.
questions.modelAnswer: The cloudy sample shows carbon dioxide is present; the clear one shows that gas is not carbon dioxide (a negative result).

questions.stem: Which splint is used for the hydrogen test?

options.text: A wet splint anywhere
options.explanation: A wet splint would not light anything.

options.text: An extinguished splint at the mouth
options.explanation: An extinguished splint cannot ignite the hydrogen.

options.text: A burning splint at the tube mouth
options.explanation: The flame meets the gas at the opening and gives the pop.

options.text: A glowing splint inside the tube
options.explanation: That arrangement is the oxygen test.

questions.stem: What sound confirms hydrogen?

options.text: A dull thud
options.explanation: No thud is part of any gas test on the syllabus.

options.text: Complete silence
options.explanation: Silence would suggest the gas is not hydrogen.

options.text: A hissing whistle
options.explanation: Hissing is not the recorded positive result.

options.text: A squeaky pop
options.explanation: The rapid burn of hydrogen with air makes the characteristic squeaky pop.

questions.stem: Why must the splint not be pushed deep into the tube?

options.text: The hydrogen needs air at the mouth to burn
options.explanation: Deep inside there is no oxygen to sustain the small explosion.

options.text: Deep insertion always breaks the tube
options.explanation: The reasoning is chemical, about air supply, not about breakage.

options.text: The gas would escape faster
options.explanation: Escape speed is not the reason the pop needs the mouth.

options.text: The pop would be too loud
options.explanation: Loudness is not a safety constraint in the method.

questions.stem: What does a glowing splint do in oxygen?

options.text: Melts the tube
options.explanation: No such effect occurs in the test.

options.text: Relights
options.explanation: Pure oxygen rekindles the ember into a flame.

options.text: Goes out immediately
options.explanation: That is what happens in gases like nitrogen, not oxygen.

options.text: Turns the flame green
options.explanation: Flame colours belong to flame tests, not to this gas test.

questions.stem: Which memory hook separates the two splint tests?

options.text: Both splints test for the same gas
options.explanation: The whole point of the pair is that the gases differ.

options.text: The sound, not the splint, decides oxygen
options.explanation: The sound belongs to hydrogen; oxygen is decided by the relight.

options.text: A ligHted splint has an H for hydrogen, a glOwing splint an O for oxygen
options.explanation: The embedded letters map each splint to its gas.

options.text: Burning means oxygen, glowing means hydrogen
options.explanation: The mapping is exactly reversed from the tests.

questions.stem: State the observation that confirms hydrogen when a lit splint is used.
questions.modelAnswer: The lit splint gives a squeaky pop at the mouth of the tube.

questions.stem: State what a glowing splint does when it is lowered into a tube of oxygen.
questions.modelAnswer: A glowing splint relights in oxygen.

questions.stem: Explain why the splint is held at the mouth of the tube in the hydrogen test.
questions.modelAnswer: The gas needs the oxygen of the surrounding air to burn, so the flame only pops where hydrogen meets air at the tube mouth; pushed deep inside there is no air to support the combustion.

questions.stem: An unknown gas gives the classic sharp sound with a lit splint, while a glowing splint lowered into it does not relight. Identify the gas and justify both readings.
questions.modelAnswer: The gas is hydrogen: the squeaky pop shows hydrogen burning rapidly to give water, and the failure to relight shows the gas is not oxygen.
